The status layer is real too: being corrected in front of work they tried hard on feels like proof they are not as capable as they want to be seen.", "pull": {"collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "Soften or withhold the real feedback to stop the tears, which feels kind but quietly tells them their work is not worth honest attention and trains them to be fragile instead of capable."}, "mentorMove": "Keep the feedback full and honest, but change the frame so correction lands as evidence you believe they can go further, not as a judgment that they fell short.", "holdFirm": ["The actual substance of the feedback stays in, including the hard parts.", "The expectation is that they engage with the correction, not just receive it."], "stayFlexible": ["How you deliver it, one to one versus written first so they can absorb it before you talk.", "How much processing time you give before you ask them to respond to it."], "forceLevel": {"level": 1, "label": "Empathy"}, "script": [{"phase": "Connection", "words": "I want to say something before we look at this. I notice feedback lands hard for you sometimes, and I get that. It means you care about the work, and that is actually the right starting point."}, {"phase": "Curiosity", "words": "Can I ask, when I mark something up, what does it feel like in that moment? Like what is the thought that comes right away?"}, {"phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is how I want to handle this together. I am going to give you my real read every time, because watered-down feedback would be a waste of your time. But you can take a minute with it before we talk it through. The goal is not to grade you as a person; it is to find the next thing your work can do that it is not doing yet."}, {"phase": "Commitment", "words": "I am holding you to real feedback because I have high standards for this work and I genuinely think you can meet them. I would not push if I did not believe that."}], "longGame": "The bigger skill here is learning to separate a correction on the work from a verdict on the person. situation: A sensitive student tears up whenever I correct their work, and I find myself softening real feedback to avoid it.
